project_scope.note: Rubus trivialis and Prunus mexicana are now canonical clickable Central Texas Rosaceae anchors, giving the learner an aggregate-drupelet branch and a single-drupe branch.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Look for stipules and a hypanthium, then identify the fruit architecture.
family_diagnostics.flower: Usually radial, often 5 sepals + 5 petals, with several to many stamens around a hypanthium.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Locally important forms include drupes, pomes, aggregate drupelets and aggregate achenes.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: The family becomes much easier once you stop at 'many stamens' and ask what the fruit becomes.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: Rosaceae is a fruit-architecture family: the flower plan repeats, but the fruit changes dramatically.

steps.title: 1 · Start with a Prunus flower
steps.look_for: Five petals and many stamens arranged around a cup-like hypanthium.
steps.why_it_matters: The hypanthium is the structural thread to learn first.

steps.title: 2 · Follow one carpel to a drupe
steps.look_for: One fleshy fruit with one hard stone/endocarp.
steps.why_it_matters: That is the Prunus-style drupe branch of Rosaceae.

steps.title: 3 · Ask the fruit question
steps.look_for: Drupe? Aggregate drupelets? Aggregate achenes? Pome?
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit architecture is the fastest route through local Rosaceae diversity.

steps.title: 4 · Keep stipules in the mental model
steps.look_for: Paired stipules at the leaf base when visible.
steps.why_it_matters: Stipules plus hypanthium help separate Rosaceae from Ranunculaceae.

steps.title: 5 · See the local bramble branch
steps.look_for: A prickly trailing cane with stipulate 3–5-foliolate leaves, a shallow hypanthium, many free stamens/pistils, and a black aggregate of drupelets.
steps.why_it_matters: Adds a real canonical local Rosaceae anchor and shows the family is much broader than Prunus drupes.

comparisons.title: Rosaceae vs Ranunculaceae
comparisons.rule: Rosaceae usually has stipules and a hypanthium; Ranunculaceae usually lacks both and commonly has free carpels directly on the receptacle.

comparisons.title: Rosaceae vs Fabaceae
comparisons.rule: Fabaceae produces a legume from one carpel; Rosaceae uses hypanthium-based fruit architectures instead.

visual_lesson.caveat: Use the shared hypanthium/many-stamen flower plan, then let fruit architecture separate the local branches: Prunus = one drupe from one carpel; Rubus = aggregate drupelets from many free carpels.

family_confusion_cleanup.field_question: Where is the hypanthium, how are the carpels arranged, and what fruit type develops?
look_here_first: Inspect a flower in side view for the hypanthium (floral cup), stamens around its rim, and carpel/ovary position; a cup alone is not definitive.
Check the leaf base for stipules when present; do not treat their absence as an absolute exclusion.
Follow fruit development: a single stony drupe, aggregate drupelets, aggregate achenes, or a pome can all belong to Rosaceae.

comparison_matrix.separate: Compare a Rosaceae hypanthium with the usually separate floral organs and free carpels on a receptacle in Ranunculaceae; inspect stipules as a supporting clue, not a universal key.

Inspect the gynoecium and mature fruit: a typical legume develops from one carpel and splits along sutures; Rosaceae includes multiple distinct fruit architectures, including a Prunus drupe from one carpel.
Do not identify by a floral cup alone: examine the stamens (often opposite petals and usually equal in number in Rhamnaceae), floral disc, ovary, and fruit anatomy against Rosaceae.

exception_locks: Hypanthium shape and degree of ovary enclosure vary; Prunus and Rubus have superior ovaries while typical pome-bearing Crataegus/Malus have inferior ovaries.
Petal count, thorniness, and many stamens are not independently diagnostic.
Some Rosaceae have reduced or absent petals; fruit anatomy and floral architecture remain important.
genus_routing_cues: Prunus: one carpel developing one fleshy drupe with a stony endocarp.
Rubus: many free carpels developing an aggregate of small drupelets.
Geum: numerous achenes, often with persistent hooked or elongated styles.
Crataegus/Malus: pome, with accessory fleshy hypanthium tissue surrounding a multi-carpellate core.
